fetched_contents.text: Is Less Really More? Economic Evaluation of Minimally Invasive Surgery Abstract Study Design: Review. Objective: A comparative overview of cost-effectiveness between minimally invasive versus and equivalent open spinal surgeries. Methods: A literature search using PubMed was performed to identify articles of interest. To maximize the capture of studies in our initial search, we combined variants of the terms “cost,” “minimally invasive,” “spine,” “spinal fusion,” “decompression” as either keywords or MeSH terms. PearlDiver database was queried for open and minimally invasive surgery (MIS; endoscopic or percutaneous) reimbursements between Q3 2015 and Q2 2018. Results: In general, MIS techniques appeared to decrease blood loss, shorten hospital lengths of stay, mitigate complications, decrease perioperative pain, and enable quicker return to daily activities when compared to equivalent open surgical techniques. With regard to cost, primarily as a result of these latter benefits, MIS was associated with lower costs of care when compared to equivalent open techniques. However, cost reporting was sparse, and relevant methodology was inconsistent throughout the spine literature. Within the PearlDiver data sets, MIS approaches had lower reimbursements than open approaches for both lumbar posterior fusion and discectomy. Conclusions: Current data suggests that overall cost-savings may be incurred with use of MIS techniques. However, data reporting on costs lacks in uniformity, making it difficult to formulate any firm conclusions regarding any incremental improvements in cost-effectiveness that may be incurred when utilizing MIS techniques when compared to equivalent open techniques. The economic burden of prescription opioid overdose, abuse, and dependence in the United States was estimated to be $78.5 billion in 2013.12 Numerous studies have demonstrated a significant decrease in postoperative pain using MIS techniques.13,14 In this context, significant advancements in postoperative pain management protocols have helped further drive down costs associated with surgical episodes of care by enabling many MIS spine procedures to be performed in an outpatient setting15 While a fair number of studies have evaluated the cost-effectiveness of MIS, definitive conclusions regarding the economic value of MIS cannot be made given the significant variability in cost comparison methodologies.16 Therefore, the primary objective of this study is to serve as a comparative overview of cost-effectiveness between minimally invasive versus equivalent open spinal surgeries. Published in final edited form as: J Spine Res Surg. 2025 Mar 26;7(1):18–25. Abstract Spinal fusion is a widely performed surgical intervention for managing degenerative spinal conditions, instability, and deformities. Traditionally, open spinal fusion has been the standard approach, offering direct visualization and access to spinal structures. However, advancements in surgical techniques have led to the development of minimally invasive spinal fusion (MISF) as an alternative, aiming to achieve comparable clinical outcomes while reducing surgical trauma, postoperative pain, and recovery time. Despite these advantages, concerns remain regarding the long-term effectiveness of MISF, particularly in terms of fusion rates, complication risks, and adjacent segment disease (ASD). This review critically examines the long-term outcomes of MISF compared to traditional open fusion, focusing on key factors such as perioperative outcomes, pain relief, functional recovery, fusion success rates, and cost-effectiveness. Perioperative data indicate that MISF is associated with reduced blood loss, shorter hospital stays, and lower infection rates but may involve longer surgical times and a steeper learning curve. Long-term clinical outcomes appear comparable between MISF and open fusion, with both techniques achieving high fusion rates and significant improvements in pain and function. However, the impact of MISF on adjacent segment disease remains inconclusive, with conflicting evidence regarding its potential biomechanical advantages. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that MISF may offer financial advantages in the long term by reducing hospitalization and rehabilitation expenses, despite higher initial surgical costs. Nonetheless, limitations in current research, including variability in study methodologies, patient selection, and surgeon expertise, necessitate further high-quality, long-term randomized controlled trials. This review synthesizes the current literature on MISF and traditional open fusion, identifies existing research gaps, and outlines future directions for optimizing surgical decision-making and improving patient outcomes. This approach has been associated with reduced blood loss, shorter hospital stays, and faster rehabilitation compared to traditional open fusion [4]. As the adoption of MISF continues to grow, it is essential to evaluate its long-term outcomes compared to traditional open techniques. fetched_contents.text: Systematic Review of Cost-Effectiveness Analyses Comparing Open and Minimally Invasive Lumbar Spinal Surgery Abstract Background Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has benefits over open surgery for lumbar decompression and/or fusion. Published literature on its cost-effectiveness vs open techniques is mixed. Objective Systematically review the cost-effectiveness of minimally invasive vs open lumbar spinal surgical decompression, fusion, or discectomy using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Methods A systematic electronic search of databases (MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library) and a manual search from the cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) database and National Health Service economic evaluation database was conducted. Studies that included adult populations undergoing surgery for degenerative changes in the lumbar spine (stenosis, radiculopathy, and spondylolisthesis) and reported outcomes of costing analysis, CEA, or incremental cost-effectiveness ratio were included. Results A total of 17 studies were included. Three studies assessed outcomes of MIS vs open discectomy. All 3 reported statistically significant lower total costs in the MIS, compared with the open group, with similar reported gains in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Two studies reported cost differences in MIS vs open laminectomy, with significantly lower total costs attributed to the MIS group. Twelve studies reported findings on the relative direct costs of MIS vs open lumbar fusion. Among those, 3 of the 4 studies comparing single-level MIS-transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) and open TLIF reported lower total costs associated with MIS procedures. Six studies reported cost evaluation of single- and 2-level TLIF procedures. Lower total costs were found in the MIS group compared with the open fusion group in all studies except for the subgroup analysis of 2-level fusions in a single study. Three of these 6 studies reported cost-effectiveness (cost/QALY). MIS fusion was found to be more cost-effective than open fusion in all 3 studies. Conclusion The studies reviewed were of poor to moderate methodological quality. Generally, studies reported a reduced cost associated with MIS vs open surgery and suggested better cost-effectiveness, particularly in MIS vs open single- and 2-level TLIF procedure. Most studies had a high risk of bias. Therefore, this review was unable to conclusively recommend MIS over open surgery from a cost-effectiveness perspective. Clinical Relevance The incidence of spinal decompressive and fusion surgey and financial constraints on healthcare services continue to increase. This study aims to identify the cost and clinical effectiveness of common approaches to spinal surgery. Level of Evidence 3a. Central stenosis typically causes neurogenic claudication, although radicular complaints are also possible. Radiculopathy from nerve root impingement can cause pain, weakness, and sensory symptoms.1 The incidence of both conditions is increasing with the aging population. Outcomes have traditionally been measured by pain or patient-reported outcome scores. Spinal surgery is a significant financial cost for health services.2 The clinical effectiveness of both laminectomy and discectomy has been extensively described in the literature.3,4 Modern budgetary constraints have led to an increased emphasis on value-based health care, but the threshold of treatment cost defined as “cost-effective” can vary across health care systems. The cost-effectiveness of the surgical management of lumbar stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis has been demonstrated in several settings, most notably from cost-utility data on decompressive surgery for lumbar disc herniation .5 TLIF was first described with the aim of treating radiculopathy, by achieving decompression and circumferential fusion of 2 or more lumbar vertebrae.6 During open posterior lumbar surgery, the paraspinal muscles are detached from their origin/insertion. In contrast, minimally invasive surgery (MIS) aims to minimize muscle injury by using a paraspinal exposure that seeks to split or dilate the muscles to reduce injury. MIS is hypothesized to be associated with better perioperative outcomes, such as lower blood loss, less surgical site infections, and shortened length of hospital stay.7 Prior work reports medium- and longer-term outcomes of MIS and open approaches.8,9 Since the first description of MIS-TLIF in 2003,10 a number of articles have compared clinical effectiveness following open vs MIS lumbar spinal surgery. However, there is an absence of good quality comparative studies. The present article aims to systematically review cost-effectiveness studies comparing MIS with open surgical procedures in the lumbar spine. Our key question was whether there was evidence of a difference in cost-effectiveness between MIS and open approaches to surgical decompression, discectomy, and fusion procedures in the lumbar spine. MIS balances higher upfront costs with potential long-term savings by shifting spending from acute surgical inputs to downstream resource uses that can reduce overall healthcare expenditure over time. The evidence points to several cost components that are typically higher for MIS: initial implant and equipment costs, specialized instrumentation, and higher upfront surgical expenses such as those seen in the PearlDiver reimbursement data, where MIS approaches had lower reimbursements than open approaches for both lumbar posterior fusion and discectomy [N1-F1]. Another source also notes that disposable supplies for endoscopic cases can be significantly greater than for open procedures [N1-R3]. This is consistent with the broader literature in the direct cost comparison, which indicates that MIS may have higher initial costs for implants and equipment, but these are often offset by lower direct costs in some studies [N1-R1][N1-R5].

Shorter hospital stays and fewer complications are central to reducing overall costs. The review evidence explicitly states that MIS is associated with reduced blood loss, shorter hospital lengths of stay, lower infection rates, and faster recovery time [N1-F1]. It also notes that MIS may lower complications and perioperative pain, which can drive down costs associated with surgical episodes of care [N1-F1]. The hospital cost comparison evidence further supports this by emphasizing that the largest cost difference between open and endoscopic procedures is often disposable supplies, while the procedural cost structure is shaped by shorter stays and fewer complications [N1-R3]. In the broader economic evaluation, shorter hospital lengths of stay and fewer complications are explicitly identified as the mechanisms through which MIS can lower care costs [N1-F1].

Long-term savings come mainly from reduced reoperations and readmissions. The long-term outcomes literature reports that 28% of open surgery patients required reoperation during minimum 5-year follow-up, whereas only 14% of MIS patients did [N3-R2]. The same source also notes that long-term clinical outcomes appear comparable between MISF and open fusion, with both achieving high fusion rates and significant improvements in pain and function [N3-F3]. The readmission literature adds that 30-day readmission rates vary widely but are an important outcome measure in spine surgery [N2-R2]. The review on long-term reoperation and readmissions also emphasizes that monitoring longer-term outcomes is required to better understand the full cost impact [N3-R4]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that MIS can reduce the downstream burden of reoperations and unplanned readmissions, which in turn lowers overall healthcare costs by avoiding repeated hospitalizations, complications, and extended recovery cycles [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R4].

In short, MIS’s initial cost burden is concentrated in implants, equipment, and learning-curve-related expenses [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1], but it can offset these with shorter hospitalization, fewer complications, and lower direct surgical costs [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Long-term savings are then derived from fewer reoperations and readmissions, which reduce recurring resource use and improve the long-term cost profile [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R4].

Reimbursement and payer policy affect MIS adoption and perceived value by creating an alignment tension between short-term surgical costs and long-term savings. The evidence suggests that reimbursement is not always aligned with long-term savings. In the PearlDiver reimbursement data, MIS approaches had lower reimbursements than open approaches for both lumbar posterior fusion and discectomy [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly notes that cost reporting in MIS literature is sparse and methodology is inconsistent, making firm conclusions about incremental cost-effectiveness difficult [N1-F1]. This matters because payers often base coverage decisions on immediate reimbursement patterns rather than longer-term cost savings, which can create a misalignment between surgical value and payment structure [N1-F1].

Payers evaluate cost-effectiveness versus clinical benefit through a mix of direct costs and broader clinical outcomes. The systematic review of cost-effectiveness analyses notes that cost reporting is sparse and methodology is inconsistent, while clinical effectiveness is also an important dimension [N1-F1]. The payer perspective literature adds that from the payer’s viewpoint, costs include payments to the hospital and physicians, while societal perspectives include broader costs [N4-R4]. This means payers are especially concerned with whether MIS generates measurable savings in hospital payments, physician fees, and complications, rather than only with patient-reported improvement [N4-R4]. The review also highlights that studies reported reduced costs associated with MIS vs open surgery and suggested better cost-effectiveness, especially for single- and 2-level TLIF procedures [N5-F2]. However, it also notes that most studies had a high risk of bias, so payers may remain cautious about adopting MIS unless evidence is robust [N5-F2].

Policy and coverage decisions depend on evidence that is both methodologically sound and clinically meaningful. The systematic review concludes that the evidence base is poor to moderate in quality and unable to conclusively recommend MIS over open surgery from a cost-effectiveness perspective [N5-F2]. The economics of MIS literature similarly states that cost-effectiveness has been shown for lumbar discectomy, decompressive laminectomy, and for some fusion procedures, but the evidence remains mixed [N4-R5]. This means coverage decisions often depend on whether studies can demonstrate consistent reductions in direct costs, fewer complications, shorter hospital stays, and fewer reoperations, which are all relevant to payer value assessment [N4-R4][N5-F2]. Overall, reimbursement and payer policy are shaped by whether the evidence base can demonstrate that MIS’s long-term savings outweigh its higher upfront costs in a way that is measurable, replicable, and clinically justified [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F2].

Clinical outcomes shape perceived cost-effectiveness by determining whether the initial costs of MIS are justified by downstream resource savings and improved patient value. The most important outcome measures for cost-effectiveness are perioperative outcomes such as blood loss, infection rates, length of stay, and reoperation rates, as well as long-term functional and pain outcomes [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The long-term outcomes evidence explicitly states that long-term clinical outcomes appear comparable between MISF and open fusion, with both achieving high fusion rates and significant improvements in pain and function [N3-F3]. It also notes that perioperative data indicate reduced blood loss, shorter hospital stays, and lower infection rates, while longer surgical times and a steeper learning curve remain key considerations [N3-F3]. These findings are central because cost-effectiveness is often evaluated by whether a procedure avoids complications, reduces hospitalization, and preserves function over time [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Improved function and quality of life contribute to cost savings by reducing the need for additional interventions and resource use. The long-term outcomes evidence emphasizes that MISF may reduce hospitalization and rehabilitation expenses despite higher initial surgical costs [N3-F3]. The broader economic evaluation also notes that MIS may offset higher costs by lowering complications, infections, hospital length of stay, estimated blood loss, and recovery time [N1-F1]. The patient-reported outcomes literature adds that quality-of-life and functional outcomes are major categories of PROMs in spine surgery [N6-R4], and that patient-reported outcomes are increasingly used to measure outcome value [N6-R3]. This means that better function and quality of life are not just clinical benefits but also cost-relevant benefits, because they can reduce subsequent care needs and improve return to function [N6-R3][N6-R4].

Adverse events and reoperations can offset initial savings if they increase downstream resource use. The long-term reoperation literature reports that 28% of open surgery patients required reoperation during minimum 5-year follow-up, whereas only 14% of MIS patients did [N3-R2]. The same source also notes that long-term outcomes are important because the evidence on reoperation and readmissions is often limited, and longer-term monitoring is needed [N3-R4]. The economic review similarly highlights that the evidence base is mixed and that cost-effectiveness depends on consistent reductions in costs rather than isolated surgical advantages [N5-F2]. In other words, if adverse events or reoperations are frequent, the initial savings from shorter stays and fewer complications may be eroded, and the perceived cost-effectiveness of MIS can weaken [N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-F2].

The systematic review explicitly states that cost-effectiveness has been shown for lumbar discectomy, decompressive laminectomy, and for some fusion procedures, and that cost per QALY gained is one common valuation method [N4-R5]. This means that even if MIS does not reduce direct costs immediately, its functional and quality-of-life benefits can be incorporated into cost-effectiveness models as savings in terms of lost productivity, disability, and future care use [N4-R5]. The patient-reported outcomes literature further supports this by showing that PROMs are increasingly used to measure outcome value in spine surgery [N6-R3]. In sum, long-term quality of life and functional outcomes are not just clinical endpoints; they are important inputs into cost-effectiveness models because they can represent real resource savings and value gains [N6-R3][N6-R4][N4-R5].

## Integrated final synthesis of how MIS balances higher costs with long-term cost-effectiveness

Minimally invasive spine surgery (MIS) approaches balance their initially higher costs with potential long-term cost-effectiveness by shifting spending from acute surgical inputs to downstream resource uses that can reduce overall healthcare expenditure over time. The evidence shows that MIS often has higher upfront costs, but these are concentrated in implant and equipment expenses, specialized instrumentation, and reimbursement patterns that can differ from open surgery [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-R5]. At the same time, MIS is associated with shorter hospital stays, fewer complications, and faster recovery, which are key drivers of lower overall care costs [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Long-term savings come primarily from reduced reoperations and readmissions, with the evidence reporting that 28% of open surgery patients required reoperation during minimum 5-year follow-up, compared with only 14% of MIS patients [N3-R2]. The readmission literature also shows that unplanned readmission rates vary widely, further emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring in evaluating cost impact [N2-R2][N3-R4]. Taken together, MIS’s cost structure is higher in the short term, but its downstream savings can improve the overall cost profile if complications, hospital stays, and reoperation rates are reduced [N1-F1][N3-R2][N2-R2].

### 1) Which cost components are higher for MIS, and why?

The main cost components that are higher for MIS are implants, equipment, and reimbursement-related inputs. The evidence notes that MIS procedures may have higher initial costs for implants and equipment, and that disposable supplies for endoscopic cases can be significantly greater than for open procedures [N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-F1]. Another source explicitly states that MIS approaches had lower reimbursements than open approaches for both lumbar posterior fusion and discectomy in PearlDiver data [N1-F1]. This combination reflects both the technical complexity of MIS and the fact that reimbursement is not always aligned with long-term savings, because payers often base coverage decisions on immediate payment patterns rather than future resource use [N1-F1][N4-R4].

### 2) How shorter hospital stays and fewer complications reduce overall costs?

Shorter hospital stays and fewer complications are central to reducing overall costs. The review evidence explicitly states that MIS is associated with reduced blood loss, shorter hospital lengths of stay, lower infection rates, and faster recovery time [N1-F1]. It also notes that MIS may lower complications and perioperative pain, which can drive down costs associated with surgical episodes of care [N1-F1]. The hospital cost comparison evidence further supports this by emphasizing that the largest cost difference between open and endoscopic procedures is often disposable supplies, while the procedural cost structure is shaped by shorter stays and fewer complications [N1-R3]. In other words, MIS’s direct cost burden is offset by fewer acute resource uses and lower complication-related costs [N1-F1][N1-R3].

### 3) What long-term savings come from reduced reoperations and readmissions?

Long-term savings come mainly from reduced reoperations and readmissions. The long-term outcomes literature reports that 28% of open surgery patients required reoperation during minimum 5-year follow-up, whereas only 14% of MIS patients did [N3-R2]. The same source also notes that long-term clinical outcomes appear comparable between MISF and open fusion, with both achieving high fusion rates and significant improvements in pain and function [N3-F3]. The readmission literature adds that 30-day readmission rates vary widely but are an important outcome measure in spine surgery [N2-R2]. The review on long-term reoperation and readmissions also emphasizes that monitoring longer-term outcomes is required to better understand the full cost impact [N3-R4]. Taken together, these findings suggest that MIS can reduce the downstream burden of reoperations and unplanned readmissions, which in turn lowers overall healthcare costs by avoiding repeated hospitalizations, complications, and extended recovery cycles [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R4].

### 4) How clinical outcomes shape perceived cost-effectiveness?

Clinical outcomes shape perceived cost-effectiveness by determining whether the initial costs of MIS are justified by downstream resource savings and improved patient value. The most important outcome measures for cost-effectiveness are perioperative outcomes such as blood loss, infection rates, length of stay, and reoperation rates, as well as long-term functional and pain outcomes [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The long-term outcomes evidence explicitly states that long-term clinical outcomes appear comparable between MISF and open fusion, with both achieving high fusion rates and significant improvements in pain and function [N3-F3]. It also notes that perioperative data indicate reduced blood loss, shorter hospital stays, lower infection rates, and faster recovery time [N3-F3]. These findings are central because cost-effectiveness is often evaluated by whether a procedure avoids complications, reduces hospitalization, and preserves function over time [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Improved function and quality of life contribute to cost savings by reducing the need for additional interventions and resource use. The long-term outcomes evidence emphasizes that MISF may reduce hospitalization and rehabilitation expenses despite higher initial surgical costs [N3-F3]. The broader economic evaluation also notes that MIS may offset higher costs by lowering complications, infections, hospital length of stay, and recovery time [N1-F1]. The patient-reported outcomes literature adds that quality-of-life and functional outcomes are major categories of PROMs in spine surgery [N6-R4], and that patient-reported outcomes are increasingly used to measure outcome value [N6-R3]. This means that better function and quality of life are not just clinical benefits but also cost-relevant benefits, because they can reduce subsequent care needs and improve return to function [N6-R3][N6-R4].

Adverse events and reoperations can offset initial savings if they increase downstream resource use. The long-term reoperation literature reports that 28% of open surgery patients required reoperation during minimum 5-year follow-up, whereas only 14% of MIS patients did [N3-R2]. The same source also notes that long-term outcomes are important because the evidence on reoperation and readmissions is often limited, and longer-term monitoring is needed [N3-R4]. In other words, if adverse events or reoperations are frequent, the initial savings from shorter stays and fewer complications may be eroded, and the perceived cost-effectiveness of MIS can weaken [N3-R2][N3-R4][N5-F2].

Reimbursement and payer policy affect MIS adoption and perceived value by creating an alignment tension between short-term surgical costs and long-term savings. The evidence suggests that reimbursement is not always aligned with long-term savings. Payers evaluate cost-effectiveness versus clinical benefit through a mix of direct costs and broader clinical outcomes. Long-term quality of life and functional outcomes contribute to cost-effectiveness by providing measurable resource savings and by enabling valuation in cost-effectiveness models. The evidence identifies several patient-reported outcome measures as relevant: health-related quality of life, pain, and disease-specific disability [N6-R4]. The long-term outcomes evidence states that both MISF and open fusion achieve significant improvements in pain and function [N3-F3]. It also notes that MISF is associated with reduced blood loss, shorter hospital stays, lower infection rates, and faster recovery time [N3-F3]. These functional gains are linked to less postoperative morbidity and fewer subsequent resource demands [N3-F3]. The economic evaluation likewise argues that MIS can offset higher costs by lowering complications, infections, hospital length of stay, and recovery time [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that better function reduces the downstream burden of care and improves the long-term cost profile [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Quality-of-life gains can be valued in cost-effectiveness models through quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gains and other utility-based metrics. The systematic review explicitly states that cost-effectiveness has been shown for lumbar discectomy, decompressive laminectomy, and for some fusion procedures, and that cost per QALY gained is one common valuation method [N4-R5]. The broader economic evaluation also notes that cost-effectiveness analyses often use cost per quality-adjusted life-years gained [N4-R5]. This means that even if MIS does not reduce direct costs immediately, its functional and quality-of-life benefits can be incorporated into cost-effectiveness models as savings in terms of lost productivity, disability, and future care use [N4-R5]. The patient-reported outcomes literature further supports this by showing that PROMs are increasingly used to measure outcome value in spine surgery [N6-R3]. In sum, long-term quality of life and functional outcomes are not just clinical endpoints; they are important inputs into cost-effectiveness models because they can represent real resource savings and value gains [N6-R3][N6-R4][N4-R5].

## Conclusion

Overall, MIS balances higher costs with long-term cost-effectiveness through a combination of mechanisms: higher initial costs concentrated in implants, equipment, and reimbursement; shorter hospital stays and fewer complications that reduce acute resource use; and long-term savings from fewer reoperations and readmissions. Clinical outcomes determine whether these savings materialize, with perioperative and long-term function and pain improvements playing a central role. Payer policy and reimbursement structure further shape adoption and perceived value, because short-term payment patterns may not always align with long-term savings. Long-term quality of life and functional outcomes contribute to cost-effectiveness by providing measurable resource savings and by enabling valuation in cost-effectiveness models through QALY gains and PROMs [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-F3][N3-R4][N5-F2][N4-R4][N4-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4].
